claim: Working memory and conscious perception are thought to share similar brain mechanisms.
source: Working memory and conscious perception are thought to share similar brain mechanisms, yet recent reports of non-conscious working memory challenge this view.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context for the study.

claim: Recent reports of non-conscious working memory challenge the view that working memory and conscious perception share similar brain mechanisms.
source: Working memory and conscious perception are thought to share similar brain mechanisms, yet recent reports of non-conscious working memory challenge this view.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as motivation for the study.

claim: In a spatial delayed-response task, participants reported the location of a subjectively unseen target above chance-level after several seconds.
source: In a spatial delayed-response task, participants reported the location of a subjectively unseen target above chance-level after several seconds.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in the results section.

claim: Conscious perception and conscious working memory were characterized by a sustained desynchronization in the alpha/beta band over frontal cortex.
source: Conscious perception and conscious working memory were characterized by similar signatures: a sustained desynchronization in the alpha/beta band over frontal cortex, and a decodable representation of target location in posterior sensors.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by MEG time-frequency analyses in the results section.

claim: Conscious perception and conscious working memory were characterized by a decodable representation of target location in posterior sensors.
source: Conscious perception and conscious working memory were characterized by similar signatures: a sustained desynchronization in the alpha/beta band over frontal cortex, and a decodable representation of target location in posterior sensors.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by circular-linear correlation analyses in the results section.

claim: During non-conscious working memory, the sustained desynchronization in the alpha/beta band and decodable representation of target location vanished.
source: During non-conscious working memory, such activity vanished.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by MEG analyses in the results section.

claim: The findings contradict models that identify working memory with sustained neural firing.
source: Our findings contradict models that identify working memory with sustained neural firing, but are compatible with recent proposals of 'activity-silent' working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: The findings are compatible with recent proposals of 'activity-silent' working memory.
source: Our findings contradict models that identify working memory with sustained neural firing, but are compatible with recent proposals of 'activity-silent' working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Slowly decaying synaptic changes allow cell assemblies to go dormant during the delay, yet be retrieved above chance-level after several seconds.
source: We present a theoretical framework and simulations showing how slowly decaying synaptic changes allow cell assemblies to go dormant during the delay, yet be retrieved above chance-level after several seconds.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by computational simulations presented in the results section.

claim: Prominent theories of working memory require information to be consciously maintained.
source: Prominent theories of working memory require information to be consciously maintained (Baars and Franklin, 2003; Baddeley, 2003; Oberauer, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Influential models of visual awareness hold information maintenance as a key property of conscious perception.
source: Conversely, influential models of visual awareness hold information maintenance as a key property of conscious perception, highlighting synchronous thalamocortical activity (Tononi and Koch, 2008), cortical recurrence (Lamme and Roelfsema, 2000), or the sustained recruitment of parietal and dorsolateral prefrontal regions (i.e., the same areas as in working memory; Naghavi and Nyberg, 2005) in a global neuronal workspace (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Non-conscious priming only lasts a few hundred milliseconds.
source: Experimentally, non-conscious priming only lasts a few hundred milliseconds (Dupoux et al., 2008; Greenwald et al., 1996) and unseen stimuli typically fail to induce late and sustained cerebral responses (Dehaene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Unseen stimuli typically fail to induce late and sustained cerebral responses.
source: Experimentally, non-conscious priming only lasts a few hundred milliseconds (Dupoux et al., 2008; Greenwald et al., 1996) and unseen stimuli typically fail to induce late and sustained cerebral responses (Dehaene et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Conscious perception exerts a durable influence on behavior, accompanied by sustained neural activity.
source: Conscious perception, in contrast, exerts a durable influence on behavior, accompanied by sustained neural activity (King et al., 2014; Salti et al., 2015; Schurger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Unseen stimuli may influence behavior for several seconds.
source: Unseen stimuli may influence behavior for several seconds (Bergström and Eriksson, 2015; Soto and Silvanto, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Participants recalled the orientation of a subjectively unseen Gabor cue above chance-level after a 5s-delay.
source: Soto et al. (2011), for instance, showed that participants recalled the orientation of a subjectively unseen Gabor cue above chance-level after a 5s-delay.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging suggests that prefrontal activity may underlie non-conscious working memory.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging suggests that prefrontal activity may underlie such non-conscious working memory (Bergström and Eriksson, 2014; Dutta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Delayed performance with subjectively unseen stimuli was barely above chance.
source: Delayed performance with subjectively unseen stimuli was barely above chance (Soto et al., 2011) and could have arisen from a small percentage of errors in visibility reports, with subjects miscategorizing a seen target as unseen (miscategorization hypothesis).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous research with supporting citation.

claim: Subjects reported the exact target location with high accuracy on seen trials (Mcorrect = 69.1%, SDcorrect = 17.4%; chance = 5%; t(16) = 15.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [55.2%, 73.1%]; Cohen's d = 3.7).
source: Overall, subjects reported the exact target location with high accuracy on seen trials (collapsed across visibility ratings > 1: Mcorrect = 69.1%, SDcorrect = 17.4%; chance = 5%; t(16) = 15.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [55.2%, 73.1%]; Cohen's d = 3.7).
evidence: This is a primary behavioral finding with statistical support.

claim: As subjective visibility of the target increased from glimpsed to clearly seen, there was a corresponding monotonic increase in accuracy.
source: As subjective visibility of the target increased from glimpsed (visibility = 2) to clearly seen (visibility = 4), there was a corresponding monotonic increase in accuracy (Figure 1B; ps<0.05 for all pair-wise comparisons).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Performance remained above chance even on unseen trials (rating = 1: Mcorrect = 22.4%, SDcorrect = 13.8%; t(16) = 5.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [10.3%, 24.4%]; Cohen's d = 1.3).
source: Crucially, performance remained above chance even on unseen trials (rating = 1: Mcorrect = 22.4%, SDcorrect = 13.8%; t(16) = 5.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [10.3%, 24.4%]; Cohen's d = 1.3).
evidence: This is a primary behavioral finding with statistical support.

claim: Blindsight remained substantial after a 4s-delay (Mcorrect = 21.1%, SDcorrect = 14.7%; t(16) = 4.5, p<0.001, 95% CI = [8.5%, 23.7%]; Cohen's d = 1.0).
source: This blindsight remained substantial after a 4s-delay (Mcorrect = 21.1%, SDcorrect = 14.7%; t(16) = 4.5, p<0.001, 95% CI = [8.5%, 23.7%]; Cohen's d = 1.0).
evidence: This is a primary behavioral finding with statistical support.

claim: Performance was better on seen than on unseen trials, both in terms of rate of correct responding (F(1, 16) = 198.5, p<0.001; partial η2 = 0.925) and precision (F(1, 12) = 36.7, p<0.001; partial η2 = 0.754).
source: Performance was better on seen than on unseen trials, both in terms of rate of correct responding (F(1, 16) = 198.5, p<0.001; partial η2 = 0.925) and precision (F(1, 12) = 36.7, p<0.001; partial η2 = 0.754).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support.

claim: There was neither an effect of the distractor on rate of correct responding and precision (all ps>0.079), nor any significant interactions between distractor and visibility (all ps>0.251).
source: There was neither an effect of the distractor on these measures (all ps>0.079), nor any significant interactions between distractor and visibility (all ps>0.251), indicating that distractor presence did not affect retention for seen or unseen targets.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support.

claim: Distractor presence did not affect retention for seen or unseen targets.
source: There was neither an effect of the distractor on these measures (all ps>0.079), nor any significant interactions between distractor and visibility (all ps>0.251), indicating that distractor presence did not affect retention for seen or unseen targets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Target detection d' exceeded chance-level (M = 1.5, SD = 0.7; t(16) = 8.9, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.2, 1.9]; Cohen's d = 2.1).
source: While target detection d' exceeded chance-level (M = 1.5, SD = 0.7; t(16) = 8.9, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.2, 1.9]; Cohen's d = 2.1) and correlated with accuracy and the rate of correct responding on seen trials (both Pearson rs > 0.762, both ps<0.001), there was no relationship between our participants' sensitivity to the target and any of our performance measures on the unseen trials (all Pearson rs < 0.342, all ps>0.179; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Target detection d' correlated with accuracy and the rate of correct responding on seen trials (both Pearson rs > 0.762, both ps<0.001).
source: While target detection d' exceeded chance-level (M = 1.5, SD = 0.7; t(16) = 8.9, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.2, 1.9]; Cohen's d = 2.1) and correlated with accuracy and the rate of correct responding on seen trials (both Pearson rs > 0.762, both ps<0.001), there was no relationship between our participants' sensitivity to the target and any of our performance measures on the unseen trials (all Pearson rs < 0.342, all ps>0.179; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: There was no relationship between participants' sensitivity to the target and any performance measures on the unseen trials (all Pearson rs < 0.342, all ps>0.179).
source: While target detection d' exceeded chance-level (M = 1.5, SD = 0.7; t(16) = 8.9, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.2, 1.9]; Cohen's d = 2.1) and correlated with accuracy and the rate of correct responding on seen trials (both Pearson rs > 0.762, both ps<0.001), there was no relationship between our participants' sensitivity to the target and any of our performance measures on the unseen trials (all Pearson rs < 0.342, all ps>0.179; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Target visibility predicted performance in the objective working memory task only on seen trials, but not on unseen trials.
source: Thus, target visibility predicted performance in the objective working memory task only on seen trials, but not on unseen trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Non-conscious information may be maintained for up to 4 s and successfully shielded against distraction from a salient visual stimulus, independently of overall subjective visibility.
source: Overall, these results confirm, with much higher non-conscious performance, the observations of previous studies (Soto et al., 2011): Non-conscious information may be maintained for up to 4 s and successfully shielded against distraction from a salient visual stimulus, independently of overall subjective visibility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings with reference to previous work.

claim: Subjects again chose the exact target position with high accuracy on seen trials (Mcorrect = 77.8%, SDcorrect = 13.9%) and remained above chance on unseen trials (Mcorrect = 25.6%, SDcorrect = 11.8%; chance = 5%; t(18) = 7.6, p<0.001, 95% CI = [14.9%, 26.3%]; Cohen's d = 1.7) in experiment 2.
source: Subjects again chose the exact target position with high accuracy on seen trials (Mcorrect = 77.8%, SDcorrect = 13.9%) and remained above chance on unseen trials (Mcorrect = 25.6%, SDcorrect = 11.8%; chance = 5%; t(18) = 7.6, p<0.001, 95% CI = [14.9%, 26.3%]; Cohen's d = 1.7).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support.

claim: Cue detection d' was greater than chance in experiment 2 (M = 1.7, SD = 0.8; t(20) = 10.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.4, 2.1]; Cohen's d = 2.2).
source: While, as in experiment 1, cue detection d' was greater than chance (M = 1.7, SD = 0.8; t(20) = 10.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.4, 2.1]; Cohen's d = 2.2), no correlations were observed with objective task performance on the unseen trials (all Pearson rs < 0.366, all ps>0.115; seen trials: all Pearson rs > 0.443, all ps<0.051; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: No correlations were observed between cue detection d' and objective task performance on the unseen trials in experiment 2 (all Pearson rs < 0.366, all ps>0.115).
source: While, as in experiment 1, cue detection d' was greater than chance (M = 1.7, SD = 0.8; t(20) = 10.2, p<0.001, 95% CI = [1.4, 2.1]; Cohen's d = 2.2), no correlations were observed with objective task performance on the unseen trials (all Pearson rs < 0.366, all ps>0.115; seen trials: all Pearson rs > 0.443, all ps<0.051; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Participants were better at recalling 1 rather than 5 digits in the correct order (M = 93.3% vs. 89.5%, F(1, 17) = 4.7, p=0.045).
source: As expected, participants were better at recalling 1 rather than 5 digits in the correct order (M = 93.3% vs. 89.5%, F(1, 17) = 4.7, p=0.045), irrespective of target visibility or delay duration (all ps>0.135).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support.

claim: Working memory load modulated the relationship between precision and visibility (interaction F(1, 13) = 8.7, p=0.011; partial η2 = .400), with no effect on seen (t(13) = 0.6, p=0.561) and a strong reduction of precision on unseen trials (t(13) = −3.6, p=0.004).
source: Analyzing only the trials with correctly recalled digits, we observed an impact of load on the precision with which target location was retained (F(1, 13) = 7.3, p=0.018; partial η2 = .360). Crucially, load modulated the relationship between precision and visibility (interaction F(1, 13) = 8.7, p=0.011; partial η2 = .400), with no effect on seen (t(13) = 0.6, p=0.561) and a strong reduction of precision on unseen trials (t(13) = −3.6, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support.

claim: Delay duration (0 or 4 s) did not influence the rate of correct responding (all ps>0.082).
source: Delay duration (0 or 4 s) also did not influence the rate of correct responding (all ps>0.082; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Delay duration affected overall precision (F(1, 15) = 9.3, p=0.008; partial η2 = .383) and the relationship between precision and visibility (interaction F(1, 15) = 5.2, p=0.037; partial η2 = .259).
source: It did, however, affect overall precision (F(1, 15) = 9.3, p=0.008; partial η2 = .383) and the relationship between precision and visibility (interaction F(1, 15) = 5.2, p=0.037; partial η2 = .259).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support.

claim: The interaction between delay duration and visibility was driven by higher precision on no-delay than on 4s-delay trials, exclusively when subjects had seen the target (t(15) = −5.7, p<0.001; unseen trials: t(15) = −0.6, p=0.559).
source: This interaction was driven by higher precision on no-delay than on 4s-delay trials, exclusively when subjects had seen the target (t(15) = −5.7, p<0.001; unseen trials: t(15) = −0.6, p=0.559).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from experiment 2 with statistical support.

claim: Even in the presence of a concurrent conscious working memory load, unseen stimuli could be maintained, with no detectable decay as a function of delay.
source: Overall, these results highlight the replicability and robustness of the long-lasting blindsight effect and suggest that it does not just constitute a prolonged version of iconic memory: Even in the presence of a concurrent conscious working memory load, unseen stimuli could be maintained, with no detectable decay as a function of delay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings from experiment 2.

claim: A conscious verbal working memory load diminished the precision with which non-conscious spatial information was maintained.
source: However, the systems involved in the short-term maintenance of conscious and non-conscious stimuli interacted, because a conscious verbal working memory load diminished the precision with which non-conscious spatial information was maintained.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings from experiment 2.

claim: Starting at ~300 ms and extending until ~500 ms after target onset, a response emerged over right parieto-temporal magnetometers when comparing seen and unseen trials.
source: Starting at ~300 ms and extending until ~500 ms after target onset, a response emerged over right parieto-temporal magnetometers.
evidence: This is an MEG finding describing the topography and timing of the visibility effect.

claim: The divergence between seen and unseen trials resulted primarily from a sudden increase in activity on seen trials ('ignition') in the perception (pFDR<0.05 from 384 to 416 ms and from 504 to 516 ms) and working memory task (pFDR<0.05 from 328 to 364 ms and from 396 to 404 ms).
source: This divergence resulted primarily from a sudden increase in activity on seen trials ('ignition') in the perception (pFDR<0.05 from 384 to 416 ms and from 504 to 516 ms) and working memory task (pFDR<0.05 from 328 to 364 ms and from 396 to 404 ms; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an MEG finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: The observed topographies and time courses fall within the time window of typical neural markers of conscious perception, including the P3b.
source: The observed topographies and time courses fall within the time window of typical neural markers of conscious perception, including the P3b (e.g., Del Cul et al., 2007; Salti et al., 2015; Sergent et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings with reference to previous work.

claim: Consciously perceiving the target stimulus involved comparable neural mechanisms, irrespective of task.
source: Consciously perceiving the target stimulus therefore involved comparable neural mechanisms, irrespective of task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Classification performance for visibility rose sharply between 100 and 300 ms and peaked during the P3b time window (all ps<0.007, except 100–300 ms in the working memory task, where p=0.066).
source: Decoding of the visibility effect was comparable in the two tasks (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1): Classification performance rose sharply between 100 and 300 ms and peaked during the P3b time window (all ps<0.007, except 100–300 ms in the working memory task, where p=0.066).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Classification performance for visibility decayed slowly from ~1 s onwards in both tasks, yet remained above chance during the 0.6–1.55 s interval (all ps<0.001).
source: It then decayed slowly from ~1 s onwards in both tasks, yet remained above chance during the 0.6–1.55 s interval (all ps<0.001).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: Classifiers trained in the perception task performed above chance during the first three time windows on working memory trials (and vice versa; all ps<0.014).
source: Though rapidly dropping to chance-level after ~1 s, classifiers trained in the perception task performed above chance during the first three time windows on working memory trials (and vice versa; all ps<0.014), indicating that, early on, both tasks recruited similar brain mechanisms.
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: Early on, both tasks recruited similar brain mechanisms.
source: Though rapidly dropping to chance-level after ~1 s, classifiers trained in the perception task performed above chance during the first three time windows on working memory trials (and vice versa; all ps<0.014), indicating that, early on, both tasks recruited similar brain mechanisms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG decoding findings.

claim: Classifiers trained during the P3b time window in the perception task and tested in the working memory task persisted up to ~860 ms (AUC = 0.53 ± 0.01, puncorrected=0.028).
source: Similarly, classifiers trained during the same time period in the perception task and tested in the working memory task persisted up to ~860 ms (AUC = 0.53 ± 0.01, puncorrected=0.028).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: Brain processes deployed for the conscious representation of the target were partially sustained during the working memory delay.
source: Brain processes deployed for the conscious representation of the target were thus partially sustained during the working memory delay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG decoding findings.

claim: Seeing the target entailed a similar unfolding of neural events in two task contexts: Conscious perception primarily consisted in a dynamic series of partially overlapping information-processing stages, each characterized by temporary, metastable patterns of neural activity.
source: These results confirm that seeing the target entailed a similar unfolding of neural events in two task contexts: Conscious perception primarily consisted in a dynamic series of partially overlapping information-processing stages, each characterized by temporary, metastable patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Working memory implies the prolongation of a conscious episode, and, in part, a succession of additional processing steps.
source: As such, these findings corroborate previous accounts linking conscious perception to an 'ignition' of brain activity (Del Cul et al., 2007; Gaillard et al., 2009; Salti et al., 2015; Sergent et al., 2005) and suggest that, in part, working memory implies the prolongation of a conscious episode, and, in part, a succession of additional processing steps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings with reference to previous work.

claim: A desynchronization in the alpha band (8–12 Hz) was the principal correlate of conscious perception in the perception task (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.004; seen – unseen: pclust=0.009).
source: Cluster-based permutation analyses singled out a desynchronization in the alpha band (8–12 Hz) as the principal correlate of conscious perception in the perception task (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.004; seen – unseen: pclust=0.009), with seen trials displaying a strong decrease in power (relative to baseline) compared to either the target-absent or the unseen trials.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support.

claim: Seen trials displayed a strong decrease in alpha power (relative to baseline) compared to either the target-absent or the unseen trials.
source: Cluster-based permutation analyses singled out a desynchronization in the alpha band (8–12 Hz) as the principal correlate of conscious perception in the perception task (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.004; seen – unseen: pclust=0.009), with seen trials displaying a strong decrease in power (relative to baseline) compared to either the target-absent or the unseen trials.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support.

claim: The alpha desynchronization was initially left-lateralized in centro-temporal sensors, moved to fronto-central channels and extended between ~300 and 1700 ms.
source: Initially left-lateralized in centro-temporal sensors, this effect moved to fronto-central channels and extended between ~300 and 1700 ms.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding describing the topography and timing.

claim: A similar, albeit later (500–1700 ms) and more bilateral fronto-central, desynchronization was also observed in the beta band (13–30 Hz; seen – target-absent: pclust<0.001; seen – unseen: pclust=0.01).
source: A similar, albeit later (500–1700 ms) and more bilateral fronto-central, desynchronization was also observed in the beta band (13–30 Hz; seen – target-absent: pclust<0.001; seen – unseen: pclust=0.01).
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support.

claim: No differences between the unseen and target-absent trials were found in the alpha (pclust>0.676) or beta band (pclust>0.226, apart from a short-lived, weak difference between ~0.9 and 1.3 s, where pclust=0.020).
source: No differences between the unseen and target-absent trials were found in the alpha (pclust>0.676) or beta band (pclust>0.226, apart from a short-lived, weak difference between ~0.9 and 1.3 s, where pclust=0.020), suggesting that unseen trials strongly resembled trials without a target.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support.

claim: Unseen trials strongly resembled trials without a target.
source: No differences between the unseen and target-absent trials were found in the alpha (pclust>0.676) or beta band (pclust>0.226, apart from a short-lived, weak difference between ~0.9 and 1.3 s, where pclust=0.020), suggesting that unseen trials strongly resembled trials without a target.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG time-frequency findings.

claim: When comparing seen and target-absent/unseen trials in the working memory task, a similar, but now temporally sustained, pattern of alpha/beta band desynchronization was observed.
source: Most importantly, when comparing seen and target-absent/unseen trials in the working memory task, we again observed a similar, but now temporally sustained, pattern of alpha/beta band desynchronization (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with reference to figures.

claim: Starting at ~300 to 500 ms, seen targets evoked a power decrease in central, temporal/parietal, and frontal regions in the alpha (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.003; seen – unseen: pclust=0.003) and beta band (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.009; seen – unseen: pclust<0.001).
source: Starting at ~300 to 500 ms, seen targets evoked a power decrease in central, temporal/parietal, and frontal regions in the alpha (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.003; seen – unseen: pclust=0.003) and beta band (seen – target-absent: pclust=0.009; seen – unseen: pclust<0.001).
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support.

claim: The alpha/beta desynchronization spanned the entire delay period and was specific to seen trials.
source: Crucially, this desynchronization spanned the entire delay period and was specific to seen trials (Figure 4A), with no differences in power between the unseen and target-absent trials in either band (alpha: pclust>0.729; beta: pclust>0.657) and only a couple of interspersed periods of residual desynchronization persisting in the target-absent control trials.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: No differences in power between the unseen and target-absent trials were found in either the alpha (pclust>0.729) or beta band (pclust>0.657) in the working memory task.
source: Crucially, this desynchronization spanned the entire delay period and was specific to seen trials (Figure 4A), with no differences in power between the unseen and target-absent trials in either band (alpha: pclust>0.729; beta: pclust>0.657) and only a couple of interspersed periods of residual desynchronization persisting in the target-absent control trials.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: The desynchronization originated primarily from a parietal network of brain sources.
source: No task- or visibility-related modulations in power spectra were found in occipital areas, and the desynchronization originated primarily from a parietal network of brain sources (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is an MEG source localization finding with reference to figures.

claim: Alpha/beta desynchronization is a correlate of conscious perception and a neural state common to conscious perception and conscious working memory.
source: In conjunction with the afore-mentioned results, these findings imply that alpha/beta desynchronization is a correlate of conscious perception (Gaillard et al., 2009) and a neural state common to conscious perception and conscious working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG time-frequency findings with reference to previous work.

claim: The temporal generalization matrix for the visibility decoder presented as a thick diagonal, but no discernable pattern emerged for the accuracy decoder.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, this was not the case. Whereas the temporal generalization matrix for the visibility decoder presented as a thick diagonal, no discernable pattern emerged for the accuracy decoder.
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with reference to a figure.

claim: For the visibility decoder, classification performance first rose above chance at ~148 ms (AUC = 0.54 ± 0.01, pFDR=0.023), peaked at ~640 ms (AUC = 0.58 ± 0.02, pFDR=0.001), and then decayed rapidly by ~1 s (first three time windows, all ps<0.001).
source: For the visibility decoder (see also above), classification performance first rose above chance at ~148 ms (AUC = 0.54 ± 0.01, pFDR=0.023), peaked at ~640 ms (AUC = 0.58 ± 0.02, pFDR=0.001), and then decayed rapidly by ~1 s (first three time windows, all ps<0.001).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: Classification for the accuracy decoder was erratic and transient: It first sharply peaked at ~180 ms (AUC = 0.55 ± 0.01, puncorrected=0.037), dropped to chance-level, and then exceeded chance between ~372 and 724 ms with a peak at 444 ms (AUC = 0.57 ± 0.02, puncorrected=0.007).
source: In contrast, classification for the accuracy decoder was erratic and transient: It first sharply peaked at ~180 ms (AUC = 0.55 ± 0.01, puncorrected=0.037), dropped to chance-level, and then exceeded chance between ~372 and 724 ms with a peak at 444 ms (AUC = 0.57 ± 0.02, puncorrected=0.007).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: The accuracy decoder rose a third time between ~1.44 and 1.74 s, peaking with similar magnitude as before at ~1.58 s (AUC = 0.57 ± 0.02, puncorrected=0.010; P3b and last time window: all ps<0.023).
source: Much unlike any of the previous decoders involving the perception task, long after the visibility response, it rose a third time between ~1.44 and 1.74 s, peaking with similar magnitude as before at ~1.58 s (AUC = 0.57 ± 0.02, puncorrected=0.010; P3b and last time window: all ps<0.023).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: The visibility and accuracy decoders had little in common, rendering it unlikely for the unseen correct trials to have simply been mislabeled.
source: Although the level of noise evident in the accuracy decoder thus precludes any definitive conclusion, the visibility and accuracy decoders had little in common, rendering it unlikely for the unseen correct trials to have simply been mislabeled.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG decoding findings.

claim: When averaging over all unseen trials in the working memory task, there was no indication of a desynchronization remotely comparable to the one on seen trials.
source: We next returned to our time-frequency analysis. When averaging over all unseen trials in the working memory task, there was no indication of a desynchronization remotely comparable to the one on seen trials (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with reference to figures.

claim: On the unseen trials, evidence for the null hypothesis (i.e., no relative change in alpha/beta power) was at least similar or stronger than evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
source: Indeed, Bayesian statistics indicated that, on the unseen trials, evidence for the null hypothesis (i.e., no relative change in alpha/beta power) was at least similar (at the very end of the epoch) or stronger than evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with Bayesian statistical support.

claim: On seen trials, evidence for the alternative hypothesis was always strongly favored.
source: By contrast, on seen trials, evidence for the alternative hypothesis was always strongly favored (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with Bayesian statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Even when analyzing the unseen correct trials separately, there was no appreciable trace of any alpha/beta desynchronization.
source: Even when analyzing the unseen correct trials separately, there was no appreciable trace of any alpha/beta desynchronization (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with reference to figures.

claim: Starting at ~1.5 s and extending until ~1.9 s, unseen correct trials exhibited a stronger increase in alpha power than their incorrect counterparts (pclust=0.040) in a set of posterior central sensors, corresponding to primarily occipital sources.
source: Only one short-lived effect, reversed relative to conscious trials, was observed in the alpha band (pclust=0.040) in a set of posterior central sensors, corresponding to primarily occipital sources: Starting at ~1.5 s and extending until ~1.9 s, unseen correct trials exhibited a stronger increase in alpha power than their incorrect counterparts.
evidence: This is an MEG time-frequency finding with statistical support.

claim: Unseen correct trials appeared to be nearly indistinguishable from the unseen incorrect and target-absent trials.
source: Unseen correct trials thus appeared to be nearly indistinguishable from the unseen incorrect and target-absent trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG time-frequency findings.

claim: A visibility decoder trained on alpha power to distinguish seen from unseen trials in the perception task and tested in the working memory task exhibited a thick diagonal, with above-chance decoding between ~180 ms and 1.18 s (first three time windows: all ps<0.016).
source: A visibility decoder trained on alpha power to distinguish seen from unseen trials in the perception task and tested in the working memory task again exhibited a thick diagonal, with above-chance decoding between ~180 ms and 1.18 s (first three time windows: all ps<0.016).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support.

claim: There was no evidence for any generalization of the alpha power visibility decoder to the unseen correct trials (all time windows: ps>0.211).
source: There was no evidence for any generalization to the unseen correct trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B; all time windows: ps>0.211).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: A visibility decoder trained on average beta power entirely failed to generalize to the unseen correct trials (all time windows: ps>0.191).
source: Similarly, a visibility decoder trained on average beta power entirely failed to generalize to the unseen correct trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C; all time windows: ps>0.191).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Converging evidence from decoding analyses in the ERFs and alpha/beta band suggests that there was no apparent discriminative axis shared between the seen and the unseen correct trials.
source: Taken together, we found a clear distinction in the brain responses of seen and unseen (correct) trials. Converging evidence from our decoding analyses in the ERFs and alpha/beta band suggests that there was no apparent discriminative axis shared between the seen and the unseen correct trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG decoding findings.

claim: The desynchronization in alpha/beta power characterizing the seen targets did not emerge on the unseen (correct) trials.
source: Similarly, the desynchronization in alpha/beta power characterizing the seen targets did not emerge on the unseen (correct) trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG time-frequency findings.

claim: These findings argue against the miscategorization and conscious maintenance hypotheses and instead suggest that non-conscious working memory is a genuine phenomenon, distinct from conscious working memory.
source: These findings therefore argue against the miscategorization and conscious maintenance hypotheses and instead suggest that non-conscious working memory is a genuine phenomenon, distinct from conscious working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Circular-linear correlations between the amplitude of the ERFs and target location revealed a strong and focal association over posterior channels, starting at ~120 ms and lasting until 904 ms (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.001; all BFs>109.60).
source: Circular-linear correlations between the amplitude of the ERFs and target location (across all working memory trials) revealed a strong and focal association (relative to a permuted null distribution) over posterior channels, starting at ~120 ms and lasting until 904 ms (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.001; all BFs>109.60; Figure 5A and Supplementary files 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Distractor position could be tracked between ~194 and 570 ms after its presentation (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.009; all BFs>14.47).
source: Similarly, distractor position could be tracked between ~194 and 570 ms after its presentation (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.009; all BFs>14.47).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: The position of stimuli could be faithfully retrieved in visual areas.
source: The position of our stimuli could thus be faithfully retrieved in visual areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG circular-linear correlation findings.

claim: Target position was transiently encoded via slowly decaying activity in occipital as well as bilateral temporo-occipital cortex from ~120 to 800 ms on seen trials (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.001 and all BFs>24.07, with the exception of the 100–300 ms period in right temporo-occipital channels, where p=0.064 and BF=2.31).
source: Target position was transiently encoded via slowly decaying activity in occipital as well as bilateral temporo-occipital cortex from ~120 to 800 ms on seen trials (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.001 and all BFs>24.07, with the exception of the 100–300 ms period in right temporo-occipital channels, where p=0.064 and BF=2.31) and in occipital and left temporo-occipital brain areas from ~180 to 504 ms on unseen trials (early time window: all ps<0.047; all BFs>2.58).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: Target position was transiently encoded in occipital and left temporo-occipital brain areas from ~180 to 504 ms on unseen trials (early time window: all ps<0.047; all BFs>2.58).
source: Target position was transiently encoded via slowly decaying activity in occipital as well as bilateral temporo-occipital cortex from ~120 to 800 ms on seen trials (early and P3b time windows: all ps<0.001 and all BFs>24.07, with the exception of the 100–300 ms period in right temporo-occipital channels, where p=0.064 and BF=2.31) and in occipital and left temporo-occipital brain areas from ~180 to 504 ms on unseen trials (early time window: all ps<0.047; all BFs>2.58).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: A clear correlation with target location was found for both seen and unseen trials.
source: A clear correlation with target location was therefore found for both seen and unseen trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG circular-linear correlation findings.

claim: The correlation with target location on unseen trials was more short-lived than on seen trials, but was of comparable magnitude during the early time window (occipital/left temporo-occipital channels: all ps>0.110 when directly comparing the correlation scores of seen and unseen trials).
source: In fact, although it was more short-lived on the latter, it was of comparable magnitude as the one observed on the seen trials during the early time window (occipital/left temporo-occipital channels: all ps>0.110 when directly comparing the correlation scores of seen and unseen trials in a Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: In the case of seen trials, both occipital and left temporo-occipital cortex maintained the target representation at least throughout the first part of the delay period (all ps<0.024; all BFs>3.77).
source: In the case of seen trials, both occipital and left temporo-occipital cortex also maintained the target representation at least throughout the first part of the delay period (all ps<0.024; all BFs>3.77), though, intriguingly, this was not accompanied by continuously sustained activity.
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: Target 'decodability' waxed and waned, appearing and disappearing periodically on seen trials.
source: Target 'decodability' instead waxed and waned, appearing and disappearing periodically.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG circular-linear correlation findings.

claim: No correlation with target location was observed for the maintenance of unseen targets during the delay period (first and second part of the delay: all ps>0.446; all BFs<0.047).
source: No such activity was observed for the maintenance of unseen targets (first and second part of the delay: all ps>0.446; all BFs<0.047).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: The absence of 'decodability' during the maintenance period for unseen targets persisted, even when considering unseen correct and unseen incorrect trials separately.
source: This absence of 'decodability' during the maintenance period persisted, even when considering unseen correct and unseen incorrect trials separately (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Posterior sensory regions may initially encode seen and unseen memoranda via slowly decaying neural activity.
source: Taken together, in line with previous research (Harrison and Tong, 2009; King et al., 2016), these results suggest that posterior sensory regions may initially encode seen and unseen memoranda via slowly decaying neural activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings with reference to previous work.

claim: In the case of conscious working memory, memoranda seem to be maintained by posterior sensory regions through an intermittently reactivated, neural code.
source: In the case of conscious working memory, these then seem to be maintained by those same areas through an intermittently reactivated, neural code (Fuentemilla et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings with reference to previous work.

claim: No periodically resurfacing activity appears to accompany non-conscious working memory.
source: In contrast, no such periodically resurfacing activity appears to accompany non-conscious working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Associations between response location and the MEG signal were primarily confined to posterior channels, with more frontal areas being recruited preferentially at the time of the response.
source: Circular-linear correlations rendered this prediction unlikely. Associations between response location and the MEG signal were again primarily confined to posterior channels, with more frontal areas being recruited preferentially at the time of the response (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: The topographical patterns of correlations with response location were highly similar to the ones observed for the correlation with target location.
source: As such, the topographical patterns were highly similar to the ones observed for the correlation with target location.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG circular-linear correlation findings.

claim: No additional regions were identified on the unseen trials for response location correlations and none of these areas showed any appreciable correlation before the presentation of the response screen.
source: Importantly, no additional regions were identified on the unseen trials and none of these areas showed any appreciable correlation before the presentation of the response screen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: Irrespective of stimulus visibility, common brain networks supported memories for the target stimulus and the ensuing decision.
source: This suggests that, irrespective of stimulus visibility, common brain networks supported memories for the target stimulus and the ensuing decision and that, in the case of non-conscious working memory, these did not come online until the response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG circular-linear correlation findings.

claim: In the case of non-conscious working memory, brain networks supporting memories for the target stimulus and the ensuing decision did not come online until the response.
source: This suggests that, irrespective of stimulus visibility, common brain networks supported memories for the target stimulus and the ensuing decision and that, in the case of non-conscious working memory, these did not come online until the response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG circular-linear correlation findings.

claim: On seen trials, response position was maintained throughout the majority of the epoch in occipital and left temporo-occipital brain areas (first three time windows: all ps<0.020; all BFs>4.16).
source: On seen trials, response position was maintained throughout the majority of the epoch in occipital and left temporo-occipital brain areas (first three time windows: all ps<0.020; all BFs>4.16).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: No correlation patterns with response position appeared in any of the posterior channels during the course of the epoch on unseen trials (all time windows: all ps>0.064; all BFs<1.32).
source: This was not the case on the unseen trials: No correlation patterns appeared in any of the posterior channels during the course of the epoch (all time windows: all ps>0.064; all BFs<1.32).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: A strong correlation with response location emerged for both seen and unseen trials during the response period (0–800 ms with respect to the onset of the letter cue).
source: In contrast, a strong correlation emerged for both seen and unseen trials during the response period (0–800 ms with respect to the onset of the letter cue).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding.

claim: Response location could be tracked with similar time courses and magnitude on seen and unseen trials in occipital, bilateral temporo-occipital, and frontal channels (all ps<0.024; all BFs>13.73; when directly comparing the correlation scores of seen and unseen targets: all ps>0.216, except for left temporo-occipital channels, where p=0.040).
source: Response location could be tracked with similar time courses and magnitude on seen and unseen trials in occipital, bilateral temporo-occipital, and frontal channels (all ps<0.024; all BFs>13.73; when directly comparing the correlation scores of seen and unseen targets in a Wilcoxon signed-rank test: all ps>0.216, except for left temporo-occipital channels, where p=0.040).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support.

claim: There was no clear correlation pattern with response location before the onset of the response screen on either the unseen correct or the unseen incorrect trials (all ps>0.096; all BFs<1.47).
source: When we further distinguished unseen correct from unseen incorrect trials, the results remained similar, though much noisier (Figure 6C): There was no clear correlation pattern before the onset of the response screen on either the unseen correct or the unseen incorrect trials (all ps>0.096; all BFs<1.47).
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: Only after the appearance of the letter cues did a correlation with response location emerge on unseen trials.
source: Only after the appearance of the letter cues did we observe a correlation with response location.
evidence: This is an MEG circular-linear correlation finding.

claim: Response location for seen targets could be tracked similarly to actual target location at least throughout the first part of the delay period (P3b time window and first part of the delay: ps<0.05).
source: Multivariate decoding analyses confirmed this picture: Whereas response location for seen targets could be tracked similarly to actual target location at least throughout the first part of the delay period (P3b time window and first part of the delay: ps<0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), no such pattern was observed on the unseen trials (all ps>0.153).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: No pattern of response location decoding was observed on the unseen trials (all ps>0.153).
source: Multivariate decoding analyses confirmed this picture: Whereas response location for seen targets could be tracked similarly to actual target location at least throughout the first part of the delay period (P3b time window and first part of the delay: ps<0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), no such pattern was observed on the unseen trials (all ps>0.153).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with statistical support and reference to a figure.

claim: The absence of decodability of response location persisted on the unseen correct and incorrect trials, even when training the regression model on the seen correct trials.
source: This absence of decodability persisted on the unseen correct and incorrect trials, even when training the regression model on the seen correct trials (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an MEG decoding finding with reference to a figure.

claim: These results are incompatible with the hypothesis that the long-lasting blindsight is only due to the conscious maintenance of an early guess.
source: Overall, these results are incompatible with the hypothesis that the long-lasting blindsight is only due to the conscious maintenance of an early guess, as, in this case, brain responses linked to the subjects' responses should have been observed shortly after the presentation of the target stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Recent modelling suggests that sustained neural firing may not be required to maintain a representation in conscious working memory.
source: Recent modelling suggests that sustained neural firing may not be required to maintain a representation in conscious working memory.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Mongillo et al. (2008) proposed a theoretical framework for working memory, in which information is stored in calcium-mediated short-term changes in synaptic weights, thus linking the active cells coding for the memorized item.
source: Mongillo et al. (2008) proposed a theoretical framework for working memory, in which information is stored in calcium-mediated short-term changes in synaptic weights, thus linking the active cells coding for the memorized item.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: Once synaptic changes have occurred, the cell assembly may go dormant during the delay, while the synaptic weights are slowly decaying.
source: Once these changes have occurred, the cell assembly may go dormant during the delay, while the synaptic weights are slowly decaying.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: At the end of the delay period, a non-specific read-out signal may suffice to reactivate the dormant cell assembly.
source: At the end of the delay period, a non-specific read-out signal may then suffice to reactivate the assembly.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Reactivation of the assembly may also occur spontaneously during the retention phase, similar to the rehearsal process postulated by Baddeley (2003), thus refreshing the weights and permitting the bridging of longer delays.
source: Furthermore, reactivation of the assembly may also occur spontaneously during the retention phase, similar to the rehearsal process postulated by Baddeley (2003), thus refreshing the weights and permitting the bridging of longer delays.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: In a noiseless model, there existed a critical value of mask amplitude, Acritical, which separated two distinct regimes.
source: In a noiseless model, there indeed existed a critical value of mask amplitude, Acritical, which separated two distinct regimes: Just as was the case for our seen trials, when Amask < Acritical, the neural assembly coding for the target spontaneously reactivated during the delay (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a simulation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: When Amask < Acritical, the neural assembly coding for the target spontaneously reactivated during the delay.
source: In a noiseless model, there indeed existed a critical value of mask amplitude, Acritical, which separated two distinct regimes: Just as was the case for our seen trials, when Amask < Acritical, the neural assembly coding for the target spontaneously reactivated during the delay (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a simulation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: When Amask > Acritical, the system evolved into a state without spontaneous activation of target-specific neurons, yet with a reactivation in response to a non-specific recall signal, mimicking unseen trials.
source: However, when Amask > Acritical, the system evolved into a state without spontaneous activation of target-specific neurons, yet with a reactivation in response to a non-specific recall signal, mimicking our unseen trials (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a simulation finding with reference to a figure.

claim: When fixing mask amplitude near Acritical and adding noise, the network exhibited both types of regimes in nearly equal proportions: 50.8% of trials were characterized by an activity-silent delay interspersed with spontaneous reactivations and 49.2% by an entirely activity-silent delay period.
source: When fixing mask amplitude near Acritical and adding noise continuously or just to the inputs, the network exhibited both types of regimes in nearly equal proportions: 50.8% of trials were characterized by an activity-silent delay interspersed with spontaneous reactivations and 49.2% by an entirely activity-silent delay period.
evidence: This is a simulation finding.

claim: Sorting the trials according to the existence or absence of spontaneous reactivations and computing the histograms of recalled target position relative to true location produced two distributions of objective working memory performance: one, in which target position was nearly accurately stored, and one, in which performance remained above chance despite a higher base rate of errors.
source: Reminiscent of our behavioral results, sorting the trials according to the existence or absence of these reactivations and computing the histograms of recalled target position relative to true location produced two distributions of objective working memory performance: one, in which target position was nearly accurately stored (Figure 7E), and one, in which performance remained above chance despite a higher base rate of errors (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a simulation finding with reference to figures.

claim: These simulations replicate the experimental findings and suggest the activity-silent framework as a likely candidate mechanism for both conscious and non-conscious working memory.
source: These simulations replicate our experimental findings (in particular Figures 2 and 5) and suggest the activity-silent framework as a likely candidate mechanism for both conscious and non-conscious working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation findings.

claim: Both conscious perception and conscious working memory shared similar signatures, including an alpha/beta power decrease, the latter spanning the entire delay on working-memory trials.
source: Both conscious perception and conscious working memory shared similar signatures, including an alpha/beta power decrease, the latter spanning the entire delay on working-memory trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Participants remained able to localize a subjectively invisible target after a 4s-delay.
source: However, participants remained able to localize a subjectively invisible target after a 4s-delay.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: There was no evidence that the long-lasting blindsight could simply be explained by erroneous visibility reports or by the conscious maintenance of an early guess.
source: We found no evidence that this long-lasting blindsight could simply be explained by erroneous visibility reports or by the conscious maintenance of an early guess.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The long-lasting blindsight likely reflects genuine non-conscious working memory.
source: It thus likely reflects genuine non-conscious working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: A single, activity-silent mechanism might support both conscious and non-conscious information maintenance.
source: Despite the inherent differences in subjective experience for conscious and non-conscious working memory, a single, activity-silent mechanism might support both conscious and non-conscious information maintenance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Irrespective of context, conscious perception and early parts of conscious maintenance involve a similar series of partially overlapping processing stages.
source: Irrespective of context, conscious perception and early parts of conscious maintenance thus involve a similar series of partially overlapping processing stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: Alpha/beta band desynchronizations have previously been linked with conscious perception and working memory.
source: Alpha/beta band desynchronizations such as these have previously been linked with conscious perception (Gaillard et al., 2009; Wyart and Tallon-Baudry, 2009) and working memory (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations.

claim: Modelling suggests that the memorized item is encoded by intermittent gamma bursts, which interrupt an ongoing desynchronized beta default state.
source: Modelling suggests that the memorized item is encoded by intermittent gamma bursts, which interrupt an ongoing desynchronized beta default state (Lundqvist et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: A decreased rate of beta bursts, once averaged over many trials, would result in the apparently sustained power decrease observed.
source: Such a decreased rate of beta bursts, once averaged over many trials, would have resulted in the apparently sustained power decrease we observed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: The mental representation formed during conscious perception was either maintained or repeatedly replayed during conscious working memory.
source: The mental representation formed during conscious perception was therefore either maintained or repeatedly replayed during conscious working memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MEG findings.

claim: The long-lasting blindsight effect does not just constitute a prolonged version of iconic memory.
source: Overall, these results highlight the replicability and robustness of the long-lasting blindsight effect and suggest that it does not just constitute a prolonged version of iconic memory: Even in the presence of a concurrent conscious working memory load, unseen stimuli could be maintained, with no detectable decay as a function of delay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Support for the activity-silent model comes from experiments in which non-specific, task-irrelevant stimuli, neutral post-cues, or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses presented during a delay restore the decodability of representations.
source: Support for this model comes from experiments in which non-specific, task-irrelevant stimuli (Wolff et al., 2017, 2015), neutral post-cues (Sprague et al., 2016), or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) pulses (Rose et al., 2016) presented during a delay restore the decodability of representations.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations.

claim: Direct physiological evidence for the postulated short-term changes in synaptic efficacies exists.
source: Direct physiological evidence for the postulated short-term changes in synaptic efficacies also exists (Fujisawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: A stimulus that fails to cross the threshold for sustained activity and subjective visibility may still induce enough activity in high-level cortical circuits to trigger short-term synaptic changes.
source: In this framework, a stimulus that fails to cross the threshold for sustained activity and subjective visibility may still induce enough activity in high-level cortical circuits to trigger short-term synaptic changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the theoretical framework.

claim: Transient non-conscious propagation of activity has been simulated in neural networks and measured experimentally in temporo-occipital, parietal, and even prefrontal cortices.
source: Such transient non-conscious propagation of activity has been simulated in neural networks (Dehaene and Naccache, 2001) and measured experimentally in temporo-occipital, parietal, and even prefrontal cortices (Salti et al., 2015; van Gaal and Lamme, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations.

claim: The memory of target location could have arisen from posterior visual maps.
source: The memory of target location could therefore have arisen from posterior visual maps (Roelfsema, 2015), although future research should test this prediction further.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation.

claim: Activity-silent mechanisms need not apply solely to prefrontal cortex as originally proposed by Mongillo et al. (2008), but constitute a generic mechanism that may be replicated in different areas, possibly with increasingly longer time constants across the cortical hierarchy.
source: Note that activity-silent mechanisms need not apply solely to prefrontal cortex as originally proposed by Mongillo et al. (2008), but constitute a generic mechanism that may be replicated in different areas, possibly with increasingly longer time constants across the cortical hierarchy (Chaudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation with citations.

claim: During a delay period, decodable representations of memorized images recurred at a theta rhythm.
source: Fuentemilla et al. (2010) also observed that, during a delay period, decodable representations of memorized images recurred at a theta rhythm.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: Single-trial analyses of monkey electrophysiological recordings in a working memory task have confirmed the absence of any continuous activity and instead identified the presence of discrete gamma bursts, paired with a decrease in beta-burst probability.
source: More recently, single-trial analyses of monkey electrophysiological recordings in a working memory task have confirmed the absence of any continuous activity and instead identified the presence of discrete gamma bursts, paired with a decrease in beta-burst probability (Lundqvist et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: Periodic refreshing of otherwise activity-silent representations could potentially serve as the neural correlate of conscious rehearsal, a central feature of working memory according to Baddeley (2003).
source: Such periodic refreshing of otherwise activity-silent representations could potentially serve as the neural correlate of conscious rehearsal, a central feature of working memory according to Baddeley (2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation with citation.

claim: Even consciously perceived items may not always be 'in mind.'
source: It also suggests, however, that even consciously perceived items may not always be 'in mind.'
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: There may be two successive mechanisms for the short-term maintenance of conscious and non-conscious stimuli: an initial, transient period of ~1 s, during which the representation is encoded by active firing with a slowly decaying amplitude, and an ensuing activity-silent maintenance via short-term changes in synaptic weights, during which activity either intermittently resurfaces (conscious case) or vanishes (non-conscious case).
source: In conjunction with prior evidence (King et al., 2016; Salti et al., 2015), our findings therefore indicate that there may be two successive mechanisms for the short-term maintenance of conscious and non-conscious stimuli: an initial, transient period of ~1 s, during which the representation is encoded by active firing with a slowly decaying amplitude, and an ensuing activity-silent maintenance via short-term changes in synaptic weights, during which activity either intermittently resurfaces (conscious case) or vanishes (non-conscious case).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations.

claim: Activity-silent retention need not necessarily be specific to working memory.
source: Such activity-silent retention need not necessarily be specific to working memory.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Recent investigations have demonstrated the existence of recognition memory for invisible cues.
source: Recent investigations have, for instance, demonstrated the existence of recognition memory for invisible cues (Chong et al., 2014; Rosenthal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations.

claim: Activity-silent representations may constitute a general mechanism for maintenance across the whole spectrum of temporal delays (from seconds over minutes/hours to days/weeks/decades), thus forming a generic property of memory.
source: Nevertheless, activity-silent representations may constitute a general mechanism for maintenance across the whole spectrum of temporal delays (from seconds over minutes/hours to days/weeks/decades), thus forming a generic property of memory.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: A specific prediction of the proposed model is that unseen correct trials should possess enough activity to modify synaptic weights in high-level cortical circuits, yet without crossing the threshold for sustained activity and consciousness ('failed ignition').
source: A specific prediction of the proposed model is that unseen correct trials should possess enough activity to modify synaptic weights in high-level cortical circuits, yet without crossing the threshold for sustained activity and consciousness ('failed ignition').
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.
